Dental Implants & Veneers — Complete Exam Guide

Everything in the training manual on implants and veneers, rewritten in plain language for someone brand new to dentistry — then turned into a self-marking question bank of 237 questions so you can find your weak spots before the exam does.

Built from Training Manual.pdf (205 pages) — implant chapter pp. 57–130, veneer chapter pp. 131–165, plus the foundation chapters, materials tables, duration table and consultation workflow that exam questions typically borrow from. Written for a treatment consultant handling international patients at Zhong'an International Dental Hospital, Huangshan.

How to use this guide

You have a week. Here's the order that works when you're starting from zero.

Day 1–2 · Read

Read Parts 1–3 straight through. Don't memorize yet. The goal is that no word is unfamiliar the second time you see it.

Day 3 · Numbers

Drill the numbers table below until you can recite it. Numbers are the easiest marks on any exam and the easiest to lose.

Day 4–5 · Test

Work the question bank in Part 5. Mark yourself honestly with the ✓ / ✗ buttons, then re-read only the sections you missed.

Day 6–7 · Speak

Say the client scripts out loud. Half of a consultant exam is how you answer a patient, not just what you know.

A note on the two "voices" you need

The manual constantly separates a basic answer (what you say to a client) from a detailed answer (what you must know internally). Exam questions love this distinction. Rule of thumb: to the client, simple words and no chemistry; to the examiner, the full mechanism.

Part 1

Foundations — the words everyone assumes you know

You cannot answer an implant question well if you're unsure what "pulp" or "alveolar bone" means. This part is short but it makes everything after it easier.

The parts of a tooth

Enamel

The hard white outer layer — the hardest substance in the human body. Protects against chewing forces and bacteria. It cannot grow back. A cavity usually starts here.

Dentin

Yellowish layer under the enamel, softer, full of microscopic tubes connected to the nerve. When decay reaches dentin the patient starts feeling cold, hot and sweet.

Pulp

The centre — nerves, blood vessels, connective tissue. Infection here means severe throbbing pain and swelling, and usually a root canal.

Root

The part below the gums that anchors the tooth in the jawbone. Front teeth usually have 1 root, some premolars 2, many upper molars 3.

Alveolar bone

The jawbone surrounding the roots. Gum disease makes this bone gradually disappear — which is exactly why implant patients so often need bone grafts.

Periodontal ligament (PDL)

A thin cushion of soft tissue connecting the natural tooth to the jawbone. Absorbs chewing force and lets the tooth move very slightly.

Why this matters for implants

An implant has no periodontal ligament — it is fused directly to bone. That's the whole reason "primary stability" and "osseointegration" are such big topics: a natural tooth has a shock absorber, an implant does not.

Types of teeth & the FDI numbering system

TypeNumberFunction
Incisors8Cutting food
Canines4Tearing food
Premolars8Crushing food
Molars12Grinding food
Total (adult)32—

Alternative names you must recognize: First premolar = first bicuspid · Second premolar = second bicuspid · Third molar = wisdom tooth.

Reading FDI tooth numbers

Two digits. First digit = which quadrant (1 = upper right, 2 = upper left, 3 = lower left, 4 = lower right). Second digit = which tooth, counting from the middle outwards (1 = central incisor … 8 = wisdom tooth).

NumberToothNumberTooth
21Upper left central incisor44Lower right first premolar

X-ray vs CBCT — and when to ask for which

Panoramic X-ray (Panorex)

Client-friendly line: "It's a full-mouth X-ray that shows all of your teeth, jawbone and wisdom teeth in a single image." Cheaper, 2D, the usual starting point.

3D Cone Beam CT (CBCT)

Client-friendly line: "It's a 3D scan that shows your teeth, bone, nerves and surrounding structures in detail before treatment." More expensive — used for implants, bone grafting, impacted wisdom teeth, full-mouth cases and some root canals.

The consultant rule

Always first ask whether the patient already has imaging. If they have either an X-ray or a CBCT, work with it. If they have neither and want implants, extractions, root canal, crowns, bridges or gum treatment — ask for a recent X-ray from a local clinic.

Do not routinely ask a patient to get a CBCT before the dentist has reviewed the case. CBCT is more expensive; the dentist decides if it's needed.

Purely cosmetic cases — whitening, veneers, minor smile design — usually need no imaging at the initial consultation, provided there are no signs of gum disease, pain or infection.

The cavity treatment ladder

Exam questions often ask "what treatment for what level of damage." Think of it as one staircase from smallest to biggest.

Damage levelTreatmentKey fact
Very early enamel weakeningFluoride treatmentApplied as gel, foam or varnish. It does not repair a hole — it only strengthens enamel before a hole forms.
Small cavityDental fillingComposite resin, tooth-coloured, one visit, lasts 5–10 years. Cheaper and repairable but wears faster.
Larger cavity, walls still strongInlayCustom restoration that fits inside the tooth. Made in the lab, so takes a few days.
Larger still, chewing cusps involvedOnlayInside the tooth plus covers part of the chewing surface.
Heavily decayed / cracked / worn / after root canalCrownA cap over the whole visible tooth. "Like putting a helmet on a damaged tooth." Does not replace the root.
Infection reached the pulpRoot canalRemoves infected pulp and seals the tooth. 1–2 visits, 30–90 min/tooth. Back teeth cost more because they have more roots and canals.
Tooth cannot be savedExtraction → implant / bridgeThis is where Part 2 begins.
The one-line difference everyone confuses

Filling = done in the mouth in one visit. Inlay / onlay / crown = custom-made in a dental lab, so the patient waits a few days. Crown covers the visible tooth; implant replaces the root as well.

Quick memory hook

Resin = cheap and soft. Zirconia = strong but a bit opaque, so it goes on crowns and back teeth. Lithium disilicate (e.max) = beautiful and translucent, so it goes on veneers and front teeth. Titanium = anything that lives inside the bone.

Procedure terminology you'll be quoted on

Simple extraction

Removing a tooth without a surgical procedure.

Extraction — erupted / mobile tooth

Removing a tooth that is visible in the mouth and may be loose or damaged.

Maxillary / mandibular wisdom tooth extraction

Maxillary = upper jaw. Mandibular = lower jaw.

Sedation wisdom tooth extraction

Removal performed with sedation so the patient feels relaxed and comfortable.

Tricky tooth extraction

More difficult because of the tooth's position, shape, condition or access.

Comfortable ultrasonic teeth cleaning

Professional cleaning using ultrasonic vibrations to remove plaque, tartar and stains.

In-office laser whitening / Philips Zoom

Professional whitening performed in the clinic; Zoom is the premium branded system.

Veneer aesthetic wax pattern design

A preview of the future smile so dentist and patient agree on shape and appearance before the veneers are made.

Sinus lift surgery

Creates additional bone in the upper jaw so implants can be placed securely.

Dental socket preservation

After a tooth is removed, bone material is placed in the socket to preserve bone for future treatment such as an implant.

Piezosurgery

Ultrasonic technology that cuts bone precisely while protecting nearby soft tissue.

Local anaesthesia vs sedation

Local anaesthesia numbs the area — patient stays awake. Sedation helps the patient relax; depending on type they may be very relaxed but not completely asleep.

Two classic patient confusions

"Will I be asleep?"Local anaesthesia numbs the area. Sedation helps you relax. Depending on the type of sedation you may be very relaxed but not completely asleep.

"Will cleaning make my teeth white?"Cleaning removes plaque and stains. Whitening changes the colour of the teeth to make them appear whiter.

Part 2

Dental Implants

Manual chapter 4, pages 57–130 — the main subject of your exam.

What a dental implant actually is

A dental implant is the most advanced way of replacing a missing tooth. Unlike a filling, inlay or crown — which only repair what's above the gum — an implant replaces both the root and the visible part of the tooth.

1Implant body (fixture)

A small screw, usually titanium, placed into the jawbone. It becomes the artificial root. A natural root is living tissue and is removed with the tooth; this screw takes over its job.

2Abutment

The connector between the implant and the crown.

3Crown

The visible tooth, made from zirconia or composite resin.

In everyday words

Think of a wall anchor. The screw sunk into the wall is the implant body. The little connector sticking out is the abutment. The picture you hang on it is the crown. Chain to remember: Crown → Abutment → Implant.

Indications — when an implant is appropriate

"Indication" = a situation where the treatment is a good recommendation. Seven, in the manual's order.

1Missing one tooth

Replaces the missing root and the missing tooth, and — the key selling point — doesn't require shaving down the neighbouring healthy teeth the way a bridge does.

2Missing multiple teeth

Several implants, or implants supporting a bridge.

3Missing all teeth

No teeth in one or both jaws → All-on-4 (a full arch on 4 implants) or All-on-6 (on 6 implants).

4Tooth cannot be saved

Severe decay · vertical fracture · failed root canal.

5Patient wants a fixed solution

"I don't want a removable denture." Implants are fixed in the bone.

6Loose or unstable denture

"My denture moves when I eat." Implants stabilize it.

7Wants better chewing function

Implants restore bite force much closer to natural teeth.

Contraindications — when it's not straightforward

"Contraindication" = a reason for caution. The single most important exam point: almost none of these are an automatic "no". Your job is never to reject a patient — it's to say the dentist will assess them.

1Uncontrolled diabetes

High blood sugar → slower healing, higher infection risk, higher implant failure risk. Normal fasting glucose 3.9–6.1 mmol/L; diabetes ≥ 7.0 fasting or ≥ 11.1 post-meal.

2Active gum disease (periodontitis)

Periodontal disease, bleeding gums, receding gum lines. Active infection must be treated first.

3Severe smoking

Impairs healing and bone integration.

4Insufficient bone

No bone = no foundation. Height < 5 mm or width < 3 mm. Solved with a bone graft or a sinus lift — lacking bone density does not automatically disqualify anyone.

5Poor oral hygiene

Causes infection around the implant site during healing. The patient must commit to brushing, flossing around the implant and regular checkups.

6Serious medical conditions

Recent heart attack or severe heart failure · uncontrolled hypertension · immune disorders such as active lupus (SLE) · serious bleeding/coagulation disorders such as haemophilia · advanced cancer · advanced AIDS · severe psychiatric or mental disorders.

7Bruxism (teeth grinding)

Signs: jaw pain, headaches, worn-down teeth; many people grind at night without knowing. Does not disqualify — the dentist prescribes a custom night guard.

8Blood pressure & age

Systolic must be under 140 mmHg and diastolic under 90 mmHg. High BP raises surgical complication risk. Implants should not be done before age 18–21.

9Pregnancy

Listed as a contraindication to elective implant surgery.

Haemophilia, in plain words

A genetic disease where blood does not clot normally. Such a patient may bleed for a long time after surgery, bleed excessively after an extraction, and carries increased surgical risk.

Script · diabetes "I have diabetes. Can I get implants?"

"Many diabetic patients successfully receive implants. The dentist will review your blood sugar control and medical history to determine whether implant treatment is appropriate."

Script · hypertension "I have hypertension."

This does not automatically mean the patient cannot receive an implant. Blood pressure should be well controlled before surgery; many patients with controlled hypertension safely undergo treatment after evaluation by the dentist or oral surgeon.

Script · bruxism "I grind my teeth at night — is that a problem?"

"Bruxism doesn't disqualify you from getting implants. The dentist will recommend wearing a custom night guard to protect your implants while you sleep."

Script · risk in general "Are there any risks when placing dental implants?"

"Today, implant therapy is an established standard for tooth replacement. It is well documented that implants are an extremely safe and successful method of treatment. Even though implants are very common, potential risks can vary depending on your health — your dentist will do a thorough assessment to see whether implant treatment is the right choice for you."

The alternative: a dental bridge — and why implants win

A bridge uses crowns on the teeth either side of the gap to hold an artificial tooth in place. It works well for a single missing tooth and needs no surgery. The catch: the dentist must file down healthy teeth to attach the crowns, which changes them permanently.

A patient may choose a bridge instead of an implant when

  • They don't have enough bone and don't want bone grafting
  • Their medical condition makes implant surgery risky
  • They want faster treatment
  • They want a lower-cost option
  • They are uncomfortable with surgery
  • The adjacent teeth already need crowns anyway, making a bridge reasonable

Benefits of implants over other options

Stability

Implants don't slip or move when you eat or talk.

Durability

They can last decades with proper care.

Bone preservation

Implants transmit chewing force into the jawbone, keeping it stimulated. Where a tooth is missing, the bone gets no stimulation and slowly recedes — and as bone shrinks, the shape of the face can change over time.

Easy maintenance

Brush and floss like regular teeth. No adhesives, no soaking routines.

Aesthetics

Looks and feels like a natural tooth — no visible difference.

No denture hassle

Traditional dentures need special adhesives and cleaning routines; implant-supported dentures eliminate these.

Delayed implant

A delayed implant means the implant is not placed immediately after the tooth is removed — the dentist waits for the extraction site to heal, usually 6 months.

Reasons: infection was present around the tooth · bone needs time to heal · bone grafting is needed · the extraction site isn't suitable for immediate placement.

Script"Do you do delayed implants at your hospital?"

"Yes. Patients usually need to come back after 6 months."

Bone grafting & sinus lift

Bone grafting (general)

Done when there isn't enough bone volume. Bone is added to increase width or height, creating stable support for the implant. Can be done before implant placement.

Sinus lift (upper jaw only)

A specific graft used in the upper back teeth area. The sinus membrane is lifted upward and bone graft placed underneath, creating enough space and bone support for the implant.

Why grafting is a problem worth avoiding

It requires additional surgery, healing takes 3–6 months, and it delays implant placement. That is precisely the gap Straumann's Roxolid material claims to fill — a stronger material means a narrower implant can be used, which may avoid grafting altogether.

Postoperative instructions — maxillary sinus lift surgery

First 1–3 days (most critical)

No nose-blowing, forceful cheek-puffing, or covering the nose when sneezing — anything that raises sinus pressure. No forceful rinsing, spitting or excessive talking within 24 hrs; swallow saliva gently. Cold compress on the cheek 15 min at a time with breaks. Cool soft foods only (porridge, noodles, eggs, tofu); nothing hot, hard or spicy; don't chew on the surgical side. No smoking or alcohol.

Within 1 week

No strenuous exercise (running, weightlifting, swimming, heavy bending). Sleep with the head slightly elevated to reduce swelling. Take antibiotics, painkillers and anti-inflammatories as prescribed. Brush gently, avoiding the surgical area.

Within 1 month

No hard food on the surgical side. Avoid diving, frequent air travel and high-pressure environments. Prevent colds and rhinitis; see a doctor for severe nasal congestion.

Seek immediate medical attention if

Persistent nasal bleeding or yellow / foul-smelling discharge · increasing facial swelling, fever, severe pain · fluid leaking from the nose when drinking or rinsing · looseness, bad odour or abnormal feeling in the surgical area.

The full mouth implant procedure, start to finish

Three stages. This sequence is prime material for ordering and matching questions.

Stage 1 · Preoperative check and assessment

Step 1
Imaging & oral examination

Checks alveolar bone density, height, width and overall jawbone condition; plus oral mucosa, periodontal condition, periodontitis and cavities.

Step 2
Physical condition examination

Three checks in order: 1. blood pressure (systolic <140, diastolic <90 mmHg) · 2. blood glucose (fasting 3.9–6.1 mmol/L) · 3. blood function test (AP/TTP within normal range). All three normal = suitable for surgery.

Step 3
Formulate a personalized plan

Six sub-steps: oral condition assessment → patient needs confirmation → economic consideration → implant brand selection → quantity and position determination → auxiliary surgical judgment (bone grafting / sinus lift).

Stage 2 · Dental implant surgery

Stage I surgery
Implant placement

Implants placed in the jawbone (All-on-4/6 technique for full arch) → temporary crown or bridge installed within 48 hours → patient recovers partial chewing function.

Healing
Osseointegration — 3–6 months

Bone grows tightly around the implant and locks it in place like a natural tooth root.

Stage II surgery
Abutment connection (if required)

The gums are incised and the abutment is installed on the healed implant.

Stage 3 · Restoration and completion

Step 1
Impression taking of abutment

A digital scan or impression is taken once the abutment is in place.

Step 2
Customize crown / bridge

The laboratory technician compares with adjacent teeth and adjusts shade, shape and colour.

Step 3
Send model to processing factory

The final restoration is manufactured and delivered.

FAQ · the question every full-mouth patient asks "If you remove 16 teeth, do I get 16 implants?"

No. Typically only 4–6 implants are placed in the jawbone. The other "teeth" are not implants — they are attached as a fixed bridge supported by those implants.

"What is a fixed bridge?"

A set of artificial teeth connected together as one piece, permanently attached to implants (or natural teeth), which the patient cannot remove. It replaces multiple missing teeth at once.

"Will a fixed bridge decay or wear out?"

It can't get cavities because it's artificial. It can wear down over time depending on material — resin wears faster, zirconia lasts longer. Good hygiene is still needed to keep gums and implants healthy.

All-on-4 vs All-on-6

Why they exist: traditional full-mouth replacement needs 10–14 implants per arch — very expensive, more surgery time, more bone required, longer healing. All-on-4/6 solves this by using fewer implants to support a full arch, reducing cost and treatment time.

FactorAll-on-4All-on-6
Implants per arch46
Support & bite-force distributionGoodBetter — more support points
Long-term stabilitySolidStronger
Best suited toPatients with bone loss; more cost-effectivePatients wanting maximum long-term stability
Exam-perfect phrasing

"All-on-6 has more implants than All-on-4. Because of this, All-on-6 provides better support, stronger bite force distribution, and more long-term stability. All-on-4 uses fewer implants, so it is usually more suitable for patients with bone loss and is more cost-effective."

Historical fact worth knowing: the All-on-4® treatment concept was introduced by Nobel Biocare in 1998.

Postoperative care — Stage I vs Stage II

Two separate instruction sheets. Golden rule to remember: Stage II reactions are milder than Stage I.

Stage I — implant placement (13 points)

1. Medication: antibiotics and painkillers as prescribed; no alcohol or smoking.
2. Bleeding: blood streaks in saliva within 24 hrs are normal; large clots or fresh bleeding → contact the surgeon. A cotton ball can apply pressure.
3. Swelling: oedema or bruising (even lips and cheeks) 2–3 days after surgery; use intermittent ice packs in the first two days to avoid frostbite.
4. Pain: subsides significantly in 2–3 days; persistent or recurring pain → seek attention.
5. Infection: increased pain, purulent discharge, recurring or worsening swelling, or unexplained fever → contact the surgeon.
6. Oral hygiene: no brushing on the day of surgery; resume gently from day 2; rinse with mouthwash twice a day starting the day of surgery.
7. Sutures: removed 7–14 days after surgery.
8. Diet: nothing to eat for 2 hours after surgery; soft food at a cool temperature; avoid chewing on the surgical side.
9. Smoking & drinking: control daily smoking, avoid excessive drinking.
10. Removable dentures: only under the doctor's guidance; wearing them without guidance may affect the implant outcome.
11. Bone graft cases: reduce wide mouth-opening and pressure on the area; avoid pressing, squeezing or massaging the graft area for 3 months; partial shedding of granular material is normal, large amounts → see a doctor.
12. Sinus lift cases: small blood streaks in nasal secretions in the first 3 days are normal; avoid forceful nose-blowing and violent sneezing; keep warm; use antibiotic nasal drops as prescribed.
13. Non-submerged implants (a metal cap or crown visible in the mouth): don't lick it with the tongue, don't bite hard objects with it, clean it after meals, return promptly if it feels loose.

Stage II — abutment connection (10 points)

1. Some pain as the anaesthesia wears off, subsiding within 1–2 days.
2. A small amount of blood streaks on day 1 is normal; avoid vigorous rinsing.
3. Soft-tissue swelling generally resolves within 1–2 days.
4. The overall reaction is milder than Stage I; simple cases usually need no anti-inflammatory medication. Blood streaks lasting more than 2 days, or sudden swelling / worsening pain / low-grade fever after 2–3 days → contact for follow-up.
5. No brushing on the day of surgery; resume on day 2 with a soft-bristled brush; keep the healing cap clean and bright.
6. Light diet; avoid hot and spicy food; no hard food on the surgical side.
7. No alcohol for 1 week. No smoking for 2 weeks — after that, no more than 3 cigarettes per day.
8. No strenuous exercise for 3 days.
9. Sutures removed 7–10 days after surgery; impressions taken 2–3 weeks after suture removal, or about 4 weeks for anterior (front) tooth restoration.
10. The healing cap may fall off before the final prosthesis is fitted — this is normal; contact the doctor promptly to reposition it.

Brand 1 · Straumann (Switzerland)

FactDetail
CountrySwitzerland — based in Basel
Founded1954
PositionSwiss premium; one of the world's top premium dental implant companies
Global presenceOperating in 100+ countries; used by thousands of dental professionals worldwide
Known forAdvanced materials, strong clinical research, highly predictable long-term implant success

Three technologies. The trick that unlocks half the exam: each one answers a different question — what it's made of, what its skin does, what shape it is.

Roxolid® = MATERIAL

Titanium–zirconium alloy: 85% titanium, 15% zirconium. Developed by Straumann in 2009; before that implants were Grade 4 titanium only. Proprietary — only Straumann has it.

SLActive® = SURFACE

A hydrophilic (water-attracting) surface that pulls blood onto the implant immediately after placement, forming a healing layer fast.

BLT = DESIGN

Bone Level Tapered. Wider at the top, narrower at the bottom — better stability, especially in soft or challenging bone.

Roxolid — why a stronger material matters clinically

Roxolid has higher tensile strength than Grade 4 titanium. Because it's stronger, dentists can use smaller-diameter implants while still handling normal biting and chewing forces. For a patient with a small jawbone, that can mean avoiding a bone graft entirely — less invasive treatment, and improved success rates. Documented in numerous clinical trials with up to 5 years of follow-up.

The logic chain in one line

Small jawbone → normally needs a graft (extra surgery, 3–6 months, delay) → or use Roxolid, which is strong enough as a narrower implant → no graft needed. If you place a normal implant in insufficient bone without grafting, it may not achieve proper stability, because an implant has a fixed diameter and needs enough surrounding bone.

BLT — how a tapered shape creates stability

Most bolts in everyday life are cylindrical — the diameter stays the same the whole way down. A tapered implant is different, and that difference is the mechanism:

  1. The narrow tip enters the prepared hole easily.
  2. As the implant goes deeper, its diameter gradually increases.
  3. The wider part pushes against the surrounding bone.
  4. This slightly compresses the bone.
  5. Bone is elastic, so the compressed bone pushes back against the implant, like a spring.
  6. The implant threads also grip the bone.
  7. Bone compression + thread engagement = a strong mechanical lock called primary stability.

Note: the dentist deliberately drills an opening smaller than the implant diameter — that's what makes the compression possible.

SLActive — how a hydrophilic surface speeds healing

After placement there is a wound around the implant site, and the body must heal and close it before bone can form. A normal implant surface takes time to attract blood and healing cells. SLActive is highly hydrophilic, so:

  • Blood spreads quickly over the implant surface
  • A clot and early healing layer form immediately
  • This healing layer creates a "friendly surface"
  • Bone cells then attach and start building new bone

Osseointegration is the word for the result: bone grows tightly around the implant and locks it in place like a natural tooth root.

Client script · Roxolid (basic answer)

"Roxolid® is a titanium–zirconium alloy developed by Straumann for dental implants. It is stronger than standard titanium and provides excellent stability in bone, even in difficult clinical conditions, helping improve long-term implant success."

Client script · BLT (basic answer)

"A tapered implant is wider at the top and narrower at the bottom. This shape helps it hold better in the bone, especially in soft or difficult bone conditions. Because of this, the implant is more stable and has a better chance of long-term success."

Client script · SLActive (basic answer)

"A cutting-edge implant surface technology that quickly activates the body's natural healing process immediately after placement. This leads to faster healing, stronger bone integration, and improved long-term implant success."

Client script · "What is Straumann Roxolid SLActive?"

"This combines Straumann's advanced Roxolid material with SLActive surface technology, which is designed to support higher strength, faster healing and excellent long-term implant success."

Manual's warning, repeated three times: do not send the detailed technical answer to a client unless they ask for more. Avoid technical descriptions unless the client is interested.

Closely associated withThe advancement of osseointegration technology

NobelReplace CC

NobelReplace is the world's first tapered dental implant, developed by Nobel Biocare in 1997. NobelReplace CC is the upgraded version featuring a conical connection ("CC").

Six marketing keywords from Nobel's own website: proven performance · enhanced aesthetics · tapered design · conical connection · platform shifting · natural-looking aesthetics.

Proven performance

Nobel launched its first tapered implant in 1997; Straumann in 2015. That gives Nobel 25+ years of clinical data on tapered designs. This does not mean Straumann's implant is not good — Straumann has extensive clinical studies and excellent success, just not 25+ years specifically on tapered design.

Platform shifting

The abutment is slightly smaller than the implant platform, creating extra space for the gums to grow — healthier soft tissue and a more natural-looking smile. Straumann has platform switching too, just marketed differently.

Conical connection

The abutment fits into the implant like a cone inside a cone, creating a tight, precise seal. Benefits: tight seal reducing bacterial leakage · improved connection stability · reduced micro-movement between components · better long-term implant performance. Straumann implants also have a conical connection.

TiUnite® surface

Anodized titanium that increases the roughness of the implant surface, with tiny grooves. Rough surface + grooves = bone cells attach more easily and grow stronger around the implant.

Nobel also uses the phrase "compromised bone situations" — useful when explaining that the implant is designed to give stability even in challenging bone conditions.

NobelActive

Launched 2008. An advanced system designed to give high primary stability, especially in challenging bone conditions, with an innovative thread design that supports immediate loading.

Five keywords: double-lead thread · sharp cutting blades · stability · aesthetics · long clinical record (15 years). Also uses the TiUnite surface.

NobelReplace CCNobelActive
Designed forNormal or moderately challenging boneMore challenging situations needing higher primary stability
Signature featuresConical connection, platform shifting, tapered designDouble-lead thread, sharp cutting blades
Clinical record~20 years~15 years
SurfaceTiUniteTiUnite
Launched1997 (CC = upgrade)2008

The neutrality rule — never rank brands

Never say

"Nobel is better." · "Straumann is better." · "You should buy NobelActive." · "Choose NobelReplace CC because it's cheaper."

Always say

"Both Straumann and Nobel Biocare are world-leading implant brands with excellent long-term clinical success. The difference lies in the materials used, design structure, and surface technology, which influence osseointegration and long-term stability. However, the best choice depends on your bone condition, aesthetic needs, and treatment plan. Our dentist will carefully evaluate your case and recommend the most suitable system to ensure the best long-term outcome for you."

Client script · "Difference between Straumann BLT and NobelReplace CC?"

"Both feature a tapered implant design that provides excellent stability, helping increase long-term success. NobelReplace CC features the TiUnite surface, designed to provide strong long-term bone stability. Straumann BLT features the SLActive surface, designed to promote faster healing and help achieve long-term implant success. However, the best choice depends on your bone condition, aesthetic needs, and treatment plan — our dentist will evaluate your case."

Titanium base, titanium framework & abutment

An abutment is the connector that joins the implant to the crown. Both the titanium base and the titanium framework are types of abutment — think of them as "titanium abutments."

Crown → Titanium Base / Titanium Framework → Implant

FactorTitanium BaseTitanium Framework
Strength & costCheaper, less strongStronger, more expensive
Crown material used with itResin — PMMA-based photopolymer (we do not use zirconia with a titanium base)Zirconia — resin isn't strong enough for a long-term final restoration and wears down
When it's usedEarly healing phase after surgery; temporary or individual implant restorationsAfter the patient returns (~6 months), for the final full-arch prosthesis
Which casesMainly All-on-4 / All-on-6Mainly All-on-4 / All-on-6
How it's madeCustom-made in-house, not bought from the manufacturerMilled from a titanium disc (blank) by a CAD/CAM machine
Why resin on the temporary and zirconia on the final

Resin absorbs chewing force, is easy to adjust and is safer while the implant is still healing. Zirconia is much more rigid and doesn't absorb force, so it would transfer higher stress to the implant during the early healing period. Once the bone has fused (about 6 months), rigidity is no longer a risk — so the final restoration is zirconia on a titanium framework.

Do 1–2 implant patients get a Ti-base or framework?

No. And they don't get temporary teeth either — they go back toothless until the final crown.

Do All-on-4/6 patients get immediate temporary teeth?

Yes — full arch or half arch, immediate loading. They do not go toothless.

Why return after 4–6 months?

To allow osseointegration (implant-to-bone healing) before the final teeth are placed.

Can a client order titanium base + zirconia crown?

No — it is not possible for us to manufacture that combination.

Part 3

Veneers

Manual chapter 5, pages 131–165 — your second exam.

What a veneer is

A veneer is a thin porcelain or composite shell attached to the front of a natural tooth to improve its appearance. It doesn't replace a tooth — it re-faces one.

People get veneers for: whiter teeth · closing small gaps · more even-looking teeth · a "Hollywood smile" makeover · fixing chipped edges.

Implant vs crown vs veneer, in one breath

Implant replaces a missing tooth including its root. Crown caps a whole damaged tooth that still has its root. Veneer covers only the front face of a healthy tooth for looks.

Indications & contraindications

Veneers have two levels of contraindication — absolute (never) and relative (maybe, with conditions). That distinction is exactly the kind of thing an exam tests.

Indications (8)

Healthy teeth · healthy gums · discoloured teeth · chipped teeth · small gaps · minor alignment issues · wants smile improvement · mild fluorosis.

Absolute contraindications (4)

Active gum disease (periodontitis) · large cavities / active decay · very little enamel remaining · severely crooked teeth.

Relative contraindications (8)

Severe teeth grinding (bruxism) · malocclusion — deep bite, edge-to-edge bite (orthodontic treatment may be needed first) · large existing fillings · moderate tooth misalignment · high caries risk · very young patients · receding gums (depending on severity) · poor oral hygiene.

Absolute vs relative — how to keep them straight

Absolute = the tooth itself can't hold a veneer (no enamel to bond to, active decay, active infection, or the shape is too far wrong). Relative = the veneer could be placed, but something about the patient's bite, habits or hygiene makes it risky or requires treatment first.

Mild fluorosis — an indication, not a disease

In mild fluorosis the teeth may have small white spots, streaks or cloudy patches. In more severe cases fluorosis causes brown stains, rough enamel or pitting. Fluoride pitting is a developmental enamel defect — it is not tooth decay and not an infection. The teeth can be perfectly healthy but look mottled, pitted, yellowish, brownish or rough. If significant, the patient may choose veneers, crowns, or whitening if the discolouration is mild.

How we make veneers — all 10 production steps

This is the section where our hospital's own workflow is tested, floor numbers included. The milling machine and lab are on the 4th floor; intraoral scanning happens on the 3rd floor.

Step 1a
Intraoral scanning (3rd floor)

The dentist scans the teeth with an intraoral scanner, capturing detailed 3D images of teeth and gums and sending the data straight to a computer. The same scanner is used for both veneers and crowns.

Step 1b
Shade selection

The dentist picks the shade using a shade guide (we also have a VITA shade guide), evaluating the patient's natural tooth colour, aesthetic expectations, and whether they want a natural or brighter smile. The shade is communicated to the lab on the 4th floor.

Step 2
CAD design (4th floor)

A digital veneer design is created in CAD software according to the patient's smile line, tooth shape and aesthetic requirements. CAD generates the exact shape and thickness, ensuring a precise fit before manufacturing.

Step 3
CAM processing — WorkNC (4th floor)

CAM software (WorkNC) converts the design into step-by-step machine instructions and plans how the veneers will be cut. The data is then transferred to the milling machine over the network.

Step 4
Milling — 10–20 minutes

A CAD block is placed inside the machine, which carves the veneer with high-speed rotating tools. Straight after milling the veneer looks white, chalky or slightly bluish, is soft, rough, has no shine and no final colour depth — the shape is accurate but it isn't finished.

Step 5
Crystallization — ~1.5 hours

The veneer goes into a ceramic furnace. During crystallization the material develops its final strength, shade, translucency and natural tooth-like appearance. The 1.5 hours is one furnace cycle, which can hold multiple veneers at once.

Step 6
Layering (optional, handcrafted)

A technician hand-applies a ceramic layer (porcelain powder) over the crystallized restoration to improve translucency, enhance colour and shade, and create natural detail. Not all veneers need layering — it's for the highest-aesthetic cases. Ivoclar's layering material is called IPS e.max Ceram. After layering, it goes back to the furnace.

Step 7
Glazing

A thin glaze layer improves surface smoothness, natural gloss and stain resistance, then a final glaze firing. Analogy from the manual: like varnishing a wooden table — without it the restoration looks dull.

Step 8
Cleaning & polishing

Residue is cleaned and the surface refined for smoothness and quality.

Step 9
Quality control

Final cleaning and inspection: surface cleaning · shade verification · fit and margin check.

Step 10
Delivery to clinic

Placed in a protective case and delivered to the dental clinic.

What a CAD block is

A pre-manufactured block of dental material used in the milling machine — the raw starting material for a veneer. For glass ceramic veneers the block is usually lithium disilicate or another advanced glass ceramic. The three brands we use:

Upcera Glass Ceramic

China

IPS e.max CAD (Ivoclar)

Switzerland

VITA Glass Ceramic

Germany

Veneer vs crown production — the difference that gets tested

Same first three steps (scan → CAD → CAM). Then: a veneer is milled from a glass-ceramic CAD block, mills in 10–20 min, and is fired for about 1.5 hours (crystallization). A crown is milled from a zirconia disc, mills in 15–20 min, and is sintered for about 11 hours. Crowns also get a bite (occlusion) adjustment using articulating paper — veneers don't have that step in the manual's list.

How veneers are placed on the teeth

  1. Take a digital scan or impression of the teeth.
  2. A dental lab makes the porcelain veneer.
  3. The dentist gently buffs or reshapes the enamel to prepare the tooth.
  4. An acid etching gel is applied to create microscopic roughness so the cement can grip strongly.
  5. A bonding agent is applied — it acts like a primer.
  6. The veneer is attached with resin cement and a curing light.

Two types of veneer

Porcelain veneers

Custom-made in a dental lab after impressions or digital scans. Bonded at a later visit. This is what we do.

Composite resin veneers

Made directly by the dentist in the office — tooth-coloured resin applied, shaped by hand, hardened with a curing light. We do not do composite veneers at our hospital.

Disadvantages of porcelain veneers (be honest about these)

  • You lose at least some natural enamel — about 0.5 mm.
  • Many types of veneer are not reversible.
  • Teeth may become more sensitive to heat and cold.
  • Gums will probably be sore for a couple of days; an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen helps.
  • Veneers need to be replaced after 10 to 15 years.
Script · client asks for composite or "no-prep" veneers

Background: composite veneers usually need no tooth preparation; porcelain veneers require removing about 0.5 mm. When a client asks for "no-prep veneers" they usually mean composite.

Do not simply say "we don't offer composite veneers" and end the conversation. Instead: explain that composite veneers are generally less durable and don't provide the same level of aesthetics; then introduce our ultra-thin porcelain veneers, which need only about 0.5 mm of preparation — minimally invasive, almost painless, more natural and longer-lasting.

The goal is to keep the conversation going, educate the client, and guide them toward the advantages of porcelain veneers.

Company profiles

Upcera — China

Originated from the Tsinghua University Ceramic Laboratory, founded 2001. Operates more than 10 subsidiaries across China, Germany and the United States; present in 110+ countries and regions.

Ivoclar — Switzerland

Founded 1923 in Zurich; headquarters in Schaan, Liechtenstein. Operates in 130+ countries with over 3,700 employees. One of the world's leading dental material manufacturers.

VITA Zahnfabrik — Germany

Full name VITA Zahnfabrik H. Rauter GmbH & Co. KG, founded 1924. One of the world's leading manufacturers of dental materials and shade-matching systems.

IPS e.max in detail

"E-max" is just a shortened name for IPS e.max. Clinics often say "porcelain veneer" when they actually mean IPS e.max glass-ceramic. The lithium disilicate glass-ceramic was introduced in 2005 and quickly became the benchmark for dental glass-ceramics. Trusted by dentists for over 20 years, with millions of successful restorations and a clinical survival rate of approximately 95%.

Why patients choose it: natural aesthetics and natural translucency (light passes through it) · high strength · proven long-term reliability.

CAD vs Ceram — one sentence

IPS e.max CAD provides the shape and strength; IPS e.max Ceram provides the beauty and natural appearance. CAD is the block that gets milled; Ceram is the porcelain powder hand-layered on top.

Client scripts · introducing the three brands

IPS e.max: "A Swiss brand offering a premium glass-ceramic veneer, widely recognized for its excellent aesthetics, translucency and long-term clinical performance." Durability 15–25 years. Always quote the price.

VITA Amber: "A premium German brand offering ceramic materials designed for highly natural colour matching, with extremely precise manufacturing for better durability — highly preferred by those looking for an ultra-natural smile." Durability 15–25 years. Always quote the price.

The most important factor, however, is selecting the material that best suits your bite, smile design and expectations — send us a few photos and our dentist can recommend the most appropriate option and explain why."

What "Top-Tier" and "Custom Luxury Handmade" actually change

What changes

Who makes the veneer (regular vs senior/master technician) · how much time is spent on customization · the level of aesthetic detailing · the amount of patient communication and personalization.

What doesn't necessarily change

The ceramic material · the basic manufacturing workflow · the layering process itself.

If a patient wants that experience, we can arrange for our most experienced technicians to be involved — the patient can even meet the technician and see the work being customized for them.

Translucency levels & bleach shades

Different people have different tooth colour and translucency. The dentist and technician must pick the right level or the restoration looks fake.

LevelMeaningUsed when
HT — High TranslucencyLets the most light through; mimics natural enamelThe natural tooth is already light or white. Best for veneers and highly aesthetic cases.
MT — Medium TranslucencyBetween HT and LTCases needing more brightness than HT but more translucency than LT.
LT — Low TranslucencyLets less light through; balances aesthetics and maskingThe underlying tooth is dark or yellow — helps block the underlying colour. Common for crowns and veneers.
MO — Medium OpacityBlocks the most lightMasking moderately discoloured teeth or metal posts.
The rule in one line

Light tooth underneath → high translucency. Dark tooth underneath → low translucency or opacity (you need the ceramic to hide what's beneath).

Bleach shades (BL shades) — IPS e.max Ceram

BL1

Brightest and whitest — commonly selected for smile makeover cases.

BL2

Slightly less bright than BL1.

BL3

Medium bleach shade.

BL4

Precautions after dental veneers

1 · Oral hygiene

Brush twice daily with a soft-bristled toothbrush and non-abrasive fluoride toothpaste. Floss daily; avoid sharp toothpicks. A water flosser removes debris gently. Clean thoroughly around the gumline.

2 · Diet & eating habits

Avoid hard foods (bones, nutshells, hard candy, ice cubes, biting into apples and carrots). Avoid tough or chewy foods (beef jerky, tough meat, sticky candy). Limit staining foods and drinks — coffee, tea, red wine, cola, curry, soy sauce; use a straw and rinse afterwards. Avoid extreme hot/cold in the first few days. Never use teeth to open bottles or tear packages.

3 · Protect against damage

Wear a night guard if you grind or clench at night. Wear a mouthguard during contact sports. Avoid nail-biting and pen-chewing.

4 · Regular dental care

Checkups and professional cleaning every 6–12 months; don't skip them — the dentist inspects veneer edges and bonding. Seek prompt care for chipping, cracking or loosening · gum pain, swelling or bleeding · persistent sensitivity · discolouration at the veneer edge.

5 · General tips

Do not use abrasive toothpaste or whitening products — they may scratch or discolour veneers. Be gentle when brushing. If a veneer comes off, keep it and contact the dentist immediately for re-bonding.

Notice the pattern across all three postop sheets

Implant Stage I, sinus lift, and veneers all repeat the same four themes: protect the site, control diet, control habits (smoking/grinding), and come back if something looks wrong. If you're asked a postop question you half-remember, answering along those four lines will usually be right.

Part 4

Around the exam — the topics that leak in

Crowns, timing, and the consultation workflow. Implant and veneer questions constantly reference these.

Crowns & crown brands

A crown is a custom-made cap covering the entire visible part of a tooth — "like putting a helmet over a damaged tooth." Needed when a tooth is heavily decayed, cracked, severely worn down, or after root canal treatment. A crown does not replace the root — the natural root stays in place and the crown covers only the visible portion above the gum line.

Common materials: porcelain (ceramic) and zirconia. Many patients specifically ask for zirconia crowns because they're strong, durable and aesthetically pleasing.

Crown production — where it differs from veneers

Steps 1–3 are identical (intraoral scan on 3rd floor → CAD → CAM/WorkNC). Then: a zirconia disc is milled (15–20 min), sintered for ~11 hours in a furnace, then polished, bite (occlusion) adjusted using articulating paper, glazed in a separate glazing room, cleaned, inspected and packed. The factory has around 18 machines, producing roughly 1,000–1,500 grams per day at full capacity.

Articulating paper shows where the bite is too high or where teeth touch too strongly — used to identify high contact points during occlusion adjustment.

The consultant workflow

Greeting a customer online

Sample greeting

"Good day Sir, thank you for contacting us. My name is XXX, and I'm a treatment consultant at Huangshan Dental Hospital. Could you please let me know about your major dental concerns?"

You can customize your greeting from experience — but keep it concise, clear, easy to understand and courteous. Always greet the customer first before starting the conversation.

Initial consultation record — the 9 questions, in order

#QuestionWhere it leads
